title: UDF & UI State Modeling
scopeHtml: Scope: the unidirectional data flow loop, how to model, produce, derive, protect and persist UI state. One-off events are chunk 03 (E1), ViewModel internals are chunk 04 (V1), Compose recomposition mechanics are A3, Flow operator mechanics are A1; this chunk cross-references them.

questions.promptHtml: What is unidirectional data flow in an Android UI, and why does Google recommend it over letting views and the ViewModel mutate each other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the base vocabulary for every architecture discussion. They want to hear a loop with named stages and a concrete bug class it removes, not "state goes down, events go up" as a slogan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "State flows in one direction: the data layer and ViewModel produce an immutable UiState, the UI only renders it, and user input goes back up as events that the state holder handles. The UI never writes the state directly. That gives a single source of truth per screen, so the screen at any moment is a pure function of one object. It removes whole bug classes like two writers disagreeing, half-updated screens and un-reproducible bugs, and it makes testing a matter of asserting on emitted states."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Start from the problem. In a classic View app, the Activity, a presenter, and a few views each held a piece of truth (a ProgressBar.visibility, a List in an adapter, a boolean in the Activity). Any of them could change any other. After a rotation you had to re-derive all of it by hand. The bug is "state lives in N places that must agree".

UDF fixes this with a loop:

   user tap / text / scroll
          |  (event, plain function call or lambda)
          v
   +----------------+   reads    +---------------------+
   |  State holder  |<---------->| Data / domain layer |
   |  (ViewModel)   |            +---------------------+
   +----------------+
          |  new immutable UiState (StateFlow)
          v
   +----------------+
   |   UI (render)  |  render(state) -> pixels. No other writer.
   +----------------+

Properties that make it work: (1) the UiState is immutable, a change is a new value; (2) there is one writer (the state holder) and many readers; (3) the UI is a function UI = f(state); (4) events are inputs to state production, not mutations of the screen. Google frames the vocabulary as "state is; events happen": state always exists and is what the UI consumes, events are transient and are the inputs to state production.

Runtime behaviour on Android: StateFlow always has a current value, so a UI that was destroyed (rotation) and re-created immediately renders the latest state. That is why UDF and ViewModel pair well: the ViewModel outlives the Activity, the state is replayed to the new UI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class CounterUiState(val count: Int = 0)

class CounterViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(CounterUiState())
    val uiState: StateFlow<CounterUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow() // read-only to the UI

    fun onIncrement() = _uiState.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1) } // event -> new state
}

@Composable
fun CounterScreen(vm: CounterViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Button(onClick = vm::onIncrement) { Text("Count ${state.count}") } // render + forward event
}

Broken: exposing MutableStateFlow publicly, or a composable doing vm.uiState.value = .... Now there are two writers and the loop is not unidirectional.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "MVVM = UDF". MVVM with two-way data binding or with the ViewModel holding a reference to the view is not UDF.
  • Exposing mutable state (MutableStateFlow, MutableList inside the state) so the UI or a child composable can write.
  • Treating UDF as a library. It is a discipline; Orbit, MVIKotlin and plain StateFlow all implement it.
  • Letting the UI keep its own copy of data "for convenience", re-creating a second source of truth.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do one-off things like navigation or snackbars fit? → Google's guidance is to reduce ViewModel-originated events to state and have the UI report consumption back (details in the one-off events section).
  2. Is UDF the same as MVI? → MVI is UDF plus a single explicit intent type and a reducer; UDF as Google describes it does not require a reducer or one intent hierarchy.
  3. What does UDF cost you? → Allocation of a new state object per change, boilerplate for events, and the temptation to put everything in one giant state; you manage those with granular state objects and stable types.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites "state down, events up". The senior names the failure it prevents (two writers, un-reproducible screens), states the single-writer and immutability invariants, and explains how StateFlow's "always has a value" semantics make rotation trivially correct.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen that kept isLoading in the Activity and items in the ViewModel showed a spinner forever after a rotation mid-request; moving both into one UiState collected from the ViewModel removed the class of bug.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between screen UI state and UI element state, and which one goes in the ViewModel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who push every mutableStateOf into the ViewModel produce chatty, hard-to-test ViewModels and lose state on navigation edge cases. It tests whether you split business logic from UI behaviour logic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Screen UI state is what to show, derived from app data, like the list of articles and loading status. It lives in the ViewModel because it must survive configuration change and is produced by business logic. UI element state is intrinsic to widgets, like whether a drawer is open, scroll position, or a text field's focus. It is owned by the UI or a plain state holder, using remember or rememberSaveable. Rule of thumb from Google: hold state as low as possible while keeping proper ownership."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Google's state-holder guidance splits logic into business logic (what to do with state changes: save a bookmark, pay) and UI behaviour logic (how to display state: scroll to an item, navigate, pick a hint string). State follows logic:

Kind Example Owner Survives rotation Survives process death
Screen UI state NewsUiState(items, isRefreshing) ViewModel (StateFlow) Yes Only what you save (Q043)
UI element state LazyListState, DrawerState, expanded flag Composable / plain class rememberSaveable where built in rememberSaveable (Bundle)

Business logic must be applied before UI logic; the UI-logic holder receives only what it needs from the business-logic holder (pass values or lambdas, not the ViewModel). A plain class state holder, such as the NiaAppState pattern in Now in Android, owns window-size-dependent UI decisions and the nav controller; it has the Composition's lifecycle, may hold Resources/NavController safely, and is not retained across Activity recreation by itself.

Why not push UI element state into the ViewModel? (1) It drags UI types (focus requesters, scroll state) toward a class that outlives the Activity: a leak risk. (2) Every keystroke or scroll tick becomes a ViewModel round trip. (3) ViewModel scope is the nav entry, but a tab's expand flag should reset with the composable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun ContactsScreen(vm: ContactsViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()  // screen UI state: business logic
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()                // UI element state: UI logic
    val showJumpToTop by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 3 } }
    ContactsList(state.contacts, listState, showJumpToTop, onRefresh = vm::onRefresh)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing LazyListState or a FocusRequester in a ViewModel.
  • Passing the whole ViewModel to child composables so any child can call anything.
  • Holding "is dialog open" in the ViewModel when it is purely cosmetic, then fighting with its reset after navigation.
  • The inverse: keeping business-driven values like isCheckoutEnabled in remember, so they vanish with the composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A dialog confirms a delete: where does showConfirm live? → If it is only UI mechanics, in the UI with rememberSaveable; if the product needs it restored identically or driven by business rules (e.g. server-requested confirmation), in UiState.
  2. Can a ViewModel depend on a plain state holder? → No, the dependency must have equal or longer lifetime; the shorter-lived holder receives data from the ViewModel.
  3. How do you test UI element state? → Plain class state holders are unit-testable without Compose; Compose-bound ones use a composition test rule (A3).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "ViewModel holds UI state". Senior: draws the business vs UI logic line, explains lifetime dependency direction, and names plain-class holders as the right home for complex UI logic like adaptive navigation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team stored a ScrollState-driven "show FAB" flag in the ViewModel and updated it on every scroll frame, causing 60 StateFlow emissions per second and a visible jank regression on low-end devices; moving it to a derivedStateOf in the composable removed the traffic.

questions.promptHtml: Should a screen expose one UiState object or several separate StateFlows? Defend a choice and say when you would change it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: There is no single right answer. They want to see consistency guarantees, recomposition cost and testability weighed against each other.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Default to one immutable UiState per screen: it is atomic, so the UI never renders a combination of values that never existed together, and it is trivial to snapshot in tests. I split into multiple flows when parts of the state change at very different rates, like a countdown timer or text field input versus a heavy list, because one big object re-emits and re-diffs everything. Even then I either compose them back into one state for the screen, or use a small number of focused state objects."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Trade-off table:

One StateFlow<UiState> Several StateFlows
Atomic consistency Yes: update { copy(a, b) } changes a and b together No: two emissions, observers can see a new and b old
Recomposition scope Any change emits a new object; readers of unrelated fields only skip if Compose can prove their parameters equal Each composable collects only what it needs
Collection cost One collector N collectors (N lifecycle subscriptions)
Testing assertEquals(expectedState, vm.uiState.value) Assert N flows, order-sensitive
Growth God-object risk Scattered state, hard to reason about

Atomicity is the senior argument. _loading.value = false; _items.value = list as two writes lets a collector observe loading=false, items=old for one frame. In Compose both are read in the same frame batch mostly, but with collectAsStateWithLifecycle on separate flows and separate dispatch, intermediate combinations are possible and show as flicker.

Skipping: a data class UiState re-emits on any field change, but Compose skips child composables whose parameters are equal (structural equality for stable types, since strong skipping for lambdas; see Q032). So pass children only the sub-fields or sub-objects they need, instead of the whole state, and a big UiState is cheap.

When I do split: text input for a search field is often a separate MutableStateFlow<String> (or TextFieldState) feeding a debounce().flatMapLatest pipeline; its keystroke rate must not rebuild the results model. The final screen state is combine(query, results) so consumers still get one consistent state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class SearchUiState(
    val query: String = "",
    val results: List<ResultItem> = emptyList(),
    val isSearching: Boolean = false,
)

@Composable
fun SearchScreen(state: SearchUiState, onQuery: (String) -> Unit) {
    SearchBar(state.query, onQuery)            // child gets only what it needs
    ResultList(state.results)                  // skipped when results is equal
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Splitting into 8 StateFlows "for performance" with no measurement, then shipping flicker from non-atomic updates.
  • A 40-field UiState with nullable everything.
  • Passing the entire UiState into every child so any change invalidates everything.
  • Using LiveData plus StateFlow mix for the same screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make a big UiState readable? → Nest sub-states (header, form, list) as their own data classes, each stable and independently equal.
  2. Can you still be atomic with several flows? → Only by combining them into one downstream flow; atomicity needs one write or one derivation.
  3. How does this change with mutableStateOf fields in the ViewModel? → Compose State per field gives fine-grained read tracking; the docs show the Compose State variant with an interface plus private mutable implementation, but you lose flow operators and non-Compose reuse (KMP, tests without Compose runtime).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average picks one by habit. Senior frames atomic consistency vs update granularity, and decomposes rather than choosing absolutely.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A trading-style screen emitted price ticks into the same UiState as the order form; every tick reset form-adjacent composables and dropped IME focus. Splitting ticks into a separate flow combined only for the price row fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: Compare modelling a screen as a sealed Loading | Success | Error hierarchy versus a data class with isLoading, error and data fields. What are impossible states and how do you avoid them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most-asked UiState question. The signal is whether you can name the failure mode of boolean flags (illegal combinations) and also the failure mode of sealed hierarchies (losing data on refresh).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A data class with three flags admits 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations when the screen has maybe 4 legal ones: loading with an error, error with no message, success and loading both true. A sealed hierarchy makes the legal states the only representable ones. But a pure sealed Loading/Success/Error loses data: refreshing replaces the list with a spinner. So for screens with refresh I model data as always present and wrap the variable parts, either Success(items, isRefreshing, refreshError) or a data class that holds a sealed content state."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Count states. With isLoading: Boolean, error: String?, items: List<T>?: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combos, and the UI must decide what isLoading=true, error="x", items=[...] means. Each developer decides differently, so bugs appear only in unusual timing.

Flags (data class)                 Sealed
  loading err items                  Loading
   T      -    -    ok               Success(items)
   F      -    S    ok               Error(message)
   T      E    -    ??? (illegal)
   F      E    S    ??? (stale + error)
   ...8 combos

But "make illegal states unrepresentable" has a limit: some of those "illegal" combinations are legitimate product states. Stale data with a refresh error (show the cached list and a banner) is real; so is refreshing with data visible. A pure sealed state forces you to drop the list during refresh and the user sees a blank screen on pull-to-refresh.

Production-grade model, two layers: the part that is mutually exclusive is sealed; the part that is orthogonal is a field.

sealed interface FeedUiState {
    data object Loading : FeedUiState                       // first load only, no data yet
    data class Error(val message: String) : FeedUiState     // first load failed, no data
    data class Content(
        val items: List<FeedItem>,
        val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
        val refreshError: String? = null,                   // stale data + inline error
    ) : FeedUiState
}

Now-in-Android style uses sealed interfaces for the screen-level state (e.g. a Loading, Success, Error family) and wraps data when needed. Use the sealed form when the screen has visually distinct modes; use a flat data class for forms and dashboards where every field is always meaningful.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun FeedScreen(state: FeedUiState, onRetry: () -> Unit) = when (state) {
    FeedUiState.Loading -> FullScreenSpinner()
    is FeedUiState.Error -> ErrorView(state.message, onRetry)
    is FeedUiState.Content -> FeedList(state.items, state.isRefreshing, state.refreshError)
}

The when is exhaustive (the compiler forces you to handle a new state), which is the second win.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• data class UiState(val isLoading: Boolean, val error: Throwable?, val data: T?) and "just check in order".
  • Holding a Throwable in state: not stable, not restorable, leaks stack text into UI. Map to a UI error type.
  • Sealed Success that cannot carry isRefreshing, so refresh wipes the list.
  • Putting dialog flags inside Success, then copying it from 5 places; extract.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get Error after Content without losing the list? → Do not transition to Error; stay in Content and set refreshError.
  2. Compose smart-cast issues with sealed state? → Read state as a local val from collectAsStateWithLifecycle delegate; it is a stable snapshot per recomposition.
  3. How do you test impossible states are impossible? → You do not need to for sealed; for the flag version, a property test generating all 8 combos shows the UI contract is undefined for 4 of them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sealed is better". Senior: counts combinations, acknowledges the stale-data/refresh case sealed alone misses, and layers sealed (exclusive) with fields (orthogonal).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed showed a blank screen on every pull-to-refresh after a refactor to a pure sealed state, increasing perceived load time in session recordings; the fix was Content(isRefreshing).

questions.promptHtml: Why do the official samples use _uiState.update { it.copy(...) } instead of _uiState.value = _uiState.value.copy(...), and why expose asStateFlow()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a short probe of concurrency awareness and encapsulation. Many candidates know the idiom but cannot explain the lost-update race.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "value = value.copy(...) is a read-modify-write. Two coroutines can both read the same old state and the second write overwrites the first one's change: a lost update. update {} runs a compare-and-set loop and retries the lambda if the value changed underneath, so it is atomic. asStateFlow() exposes a read-only view so only the ViewModel writes, which keeps the flow unidirectional."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MutableStateFlow.update(function) is implemented as a loop: read current, compute function(current), compareAndSet(current, new); on failure, repeat. Consequences:

  • The lambda can run more than once under contention, so it must be pure and cheap: no list.add, no network, no side effects.
  • Concurrent updates to different fields compose correctly: A sets isRefreshing, B sets items, both survive.

The race with .value =:

t0 state = S(count=0)
A: read S(0) ----------------> write S(1)
B:        read S(0) -> write S(1)      // B overwrote A; expected count=2

In ViewModels this is real: viewModelScope is Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so single-thread code between suspension points is atomic, but the moment any withContext(Dispatchers.IO) writes state, or two coroutines interleave across a suspension (val s = _uiState.value; val r = api.call(); _uiState.value = s.copy(r)), you have a race.

Also StateFlow is conflated and compares with equals: setting an equal value emits nothing. That is why mutating a list in place and re-setting the same list reference never updates the UI (Q048).

asStateFlow() returns a read-only wrapper (not the same object type; a cast back is not possible), unlike val uiState: StateFlow<T> = _uiState, which can be down-cast to MutableStateFlow in the UI. Use asStateFlow() for hard encapsulation (one extra tiny object).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(CartUiState())
val uiState: StateFlow<CartUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

// Broken: captured snapshot across a suspension point
fun addBroken(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
    val s = _uiState.value
    val product = repo.load(id)                       // suspends; others may update meanwhile
    _uiState.value = s.copy(items = s.items + product) // drops concurrent changes
}

// Correct: read inside update, keep the lambda pure
fun add(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
    val product = repo.load(id)
    _uiState.update { it.copy(items = it.items + product) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing the suspend call inside update { }.
  • Side effects in the lambda (logging analytics counts the retries).
  • Assuming viewModelScope makes .value = always safe.
  • Exposing MutableStateFlow to children.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is update retry safe for pure lambdas only? → Because on CAS failure it recomputes; side effects would run multiple times.
  2. Does update serialize against the collector? → No, collectors see conflated values; they may skip intermediate states.
  3. Alternative to CAS? → Mutex or confining writes to one dispatcher; for reducers, a Channel of intents processed sequentially.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "idiomatic". Senior: explains the lost-update with a timeline, says purity requirement, and ties conflation plus equality to why in-place mutation does not emit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cart badge showed 1 after adding 2 items quickly; two rapid taps each captured value before the product fetch returned. Moving the read inside update fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
Support tickets say the orders screen "shows a spinner on top of an error and sometimes loses my items". Crash-free is fine; there is no exception. 1.2M DAU, p50 network 380 ms, p95 4.1 s on 3G. Product recently added pull-to-refresh. Code:

data class OrdersUiState(
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null,
    val orders: List<Order> = emptyList(),
)

class OrdersViewModel(private val repo: OrdersRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(OrdersUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<OrdersUiState> = _state

    init { refresh() }

    fun refresh() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = _state.value.copy(isLoading = true)
            try {
                val orders = repo.getOrders()
                _state.value = OrdersUiState(orders = orders)
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                _state.value = _state.value.copy(isLoading = false, error = e.message)
            }
        }
    }
}

Screen: if (isLoading) Spinner() ; if (error != null) ErrorText(error) ; OrdersList(orders).
questions.promptHtml: List every defect you see, explain the reported symptoms, and rewrite the state model.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a finally" or "use update". They fix one race and keep 8 combinations of three flags. They miss that the catch swallows CancellationException, that OrdersUiState(orders = orders) silently resets other fields, and that the UI composes spinner and error simultaneously by design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should stale orders stay visible on refresh failure (product intent)? Is retry automatic? Does the screen survive process death with data? Are two rapid refreshes possible (pull-to-refresh plus retry button)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage; hotfix is to render error and spinner exclusively and rethrow CancellationException. Ship behind the normal release train, no rollback needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Spinner over error: refresh sets isLoading=true but keeps old error, never cleared, so both show. (b) "Loses items": the success path constructs a new OrdersUiState(orders = orders); fine here, but when two refreshes overlap the older one's failure path copies _state.value after the newer one succeeded and writes error over fresh data. (c) init { refresh() } plus a second refresh() from a LaunchedEffect on re-composition, doubling requests. (d) catch (e: Exception) catches CancellationException, so a cancelled job writes an error into state after the ViewModel is cleared or the job is replaced.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test with a fake repo using a CompletableDeferred to order two refreshes; log state transitions with uiState.onEach(::println) in test; check Layout Inspector for both composables present; grep for callers of refresh().
  5. Root cause: Three independent flags encode a state machine with 8 combinations, and the transitions are not atomic (.value = .value.copy after a suspension). There are no cancellation or in-flight-job semantics.
  6. Fix: Short term: set error = null on start, use update, rethrow cancellation. Long term: model the state, and keep one in-flight job.
sealed interface OrdersUiState {
    data object Loading : OrdersUiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : OrdersUiState
    data class Content(
        val orders: List<Order>,
        val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
        val refreshError: String? = null,
    ) : OrdersUiState
}

private var refreshJob: Job? = null
fun refresh() {
    refreshJob?.cancel()
    refreshJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { if (it is Content) it.copy(isRefreshing = true, refreshError = null) else Loading }
        runCatching { repo.getOrders() }
            .onSuccess { o -> _state.value = Content(o) }
            .onFailure { e ->
                if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                _state.update { s ->
                    if (s is Content) s.copy(isRefreshing = false, refreshError = e.toUiMessage())
                    else Error(e.toUiMessage())
                }
            }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: A state-transition unit test (Loading to Content, Content refresh failure keeps items, overlapping refresh), a lint/review rule "no isX + isY booleans for mutually exclusive modes", and Compose previews for each state.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap everything in a generic Resource<T>; it loses the refresh-with-data case. I would not add a global mutex; cancelling the older job is simpler.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if requests must not be cancelled (POST)? → Do not cancel; serialize with a Mutex or ignore taps while isRefreshing.
  • runCatching swallows cancellation? → Yes, it catches it; that is why I rethrow explicitly (A1 covers coroutine cancellation).
  • What if the repo exposes a Flow? → Then state is derived from the flow and refresh just triggers a repository refresh (Q030).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: an orders screen showed "No network" while the list below was fresh after a flaky train commute. Two overlapping refreshes finished in reverse order and the older failure overwrote newer success. Cancelling the previous job fixed it, and a deterministic test caught the regression.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds finally { isLoading = false } only.
  • Hire: Spots stale error plus non-atomic update and proposes sealed or exclusive rendering.
  • Strong hire: Identifies the overlapping-refresh ordering bug and cancellation swallowing, keeps data on refresh failure, and proposes deterministic transition tests.

questions.promptHtml: Where should derived values (totals, filtered lists, canSubmit, isEmpty) live: stored as fields in the UiState, computed properties on it, derivedStateOf in the UI, or a separate flow in the ViewModel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stored derived fields drift out of sync. Candidates should know that derived data should have one source and decide by cost and by who needs it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Never store what you can compute from other fields in the same state, because a stored copy can go stale: total updated but items not. Cheap derivations go in as computed properties on the state class. Expensive ones, like filtering or sorting 10k rows, are computed in the pipeline with combine/map off the main thread so they run once per input change, not per recomposition. derivedStateOf in Compose is for derivations from Compose state that change more often than the output, like scroll position to 'show button'."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three tiers:

  1. Computed property. val isEmpty get() = items.isEmpty(). Zero storage, always consistent, recomputed on each read. Fine when O(1) or tiny. Danger: called in a composable body it recomputes each recomposition; an O(n) filter inside LazyColumn content runs on every recomposition.
  2. Pipeline derivation in the ViewModel. combine(items, filter) { i, f -> i.filter(f) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) then stateIn. Runs once per upstream change, on a background dispatcher, and the result is part of the state, so tests assert on it. Use for sort/filter/group and anything O(n log n).
  3. derivedStateOf (UI). Compose caches the result and only invalidates readers when the derived result changes, even if the inputs change faster. Good: listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 changes every frame while the boolean changes rarely. Pointless: derived from a value that already changes at the same rate as the output.

Rule: derive as late as the consumer allows but as early as the cost requires. The consistency risk is the opposite of the cost risk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class CartUiState(
    val lines: List<CartLine> = emptyList(),
    val coupon: Coupon? = null,
) {
    val subtotal: Money get() = lines.sumOf(CartLine::lineTotal)           // cheap: computed, never stale
    val canCheckout: Boolean get() = lines.isNotEmpty() && lines.all(CartLine::inStock)
}

// Expensive: once per input change, off main
val visible: StateFlow<List<Product>> = combine(products, filter) { p, f ->
    p.filter(f::matches).sortedBy(Product::name)
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
 .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

Broken: data class CartUiState(val lines: List<Line>, val total: Money) where an update path forgets to recompute total.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing both items and itemCount.
  • derivedStateOf in the ViewModel (it is a Compose snapshot concept; works only if readers are in snapshot-aware code).
  • Computing items.filter{} directly in the Lazy list scope.
  • Putting formatted strings ("$12.50") in UiState, which forces recompute on locale change; keep Money, format in UI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Are computed properties on data classes part of equals? → No, only primary constructor properties are, which is the point: they cannot desync.
  2. derivedStateOf vs remember(key)? → remember(key) recomputes whenever key changes; derivedStateOf additionally limits invalidation to when the result changes (A3 for mechanics).
  3. How do you avoid recompute per recomposition for a computed property? → Move to the pipeline, or remember(state.lines) { state.subtotal }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put it in the ViewModel". Senior: tiers by cost, rejects stored duplicates, and knows where derivedStateOf helps and does not.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A discount bug charged the old total in analytics because total was a stored field only updated in two of five mutation paths; replacing it with a computed property deleted the bug.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through producing a screen's UiState from two repository Flows plus a user-driven filter using combine and stateIn. What does each SharingStarted option do and why does the official sample use WhileSubscribed(5_000)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the core state-production pattern in Google's guidance. They probe whether you know the upstream lifecycle, not just the syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I combine the repository flows and a MutableStateFlow for the filter into one UiState flow, then stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), Loading) to make it a hot StateFlow with an initial value. WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps upstream collection alive for 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, so a rotation, which unsubscribes and resubscribes within milliseconds, does not restart the database or network flow, while a real backgrounding stops upstream work after the timeout."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
stateIn turns a cold Flow<T> into a StateFlow<T> in a scope, with a started policy deciding when upstream is collected:

Policy Upstream collecting Use when
Eagerly Immediately, until scope cancelled Value must be ready before UI appears; cheap source
Lazily From first subscriber, never stops until scope cancelled Keep warm while screen may return (back stack, offscreen tab)
WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis, replayExpirationMillis) While subscriber count > 0, plus timeout after last leaves UI-driven streams; releases DB/socket collection when the app is backgrounded

Why 5 seconds: Google's docs and the Now in Android sample use WhileSubscribed(5_000); the stated purpose is surviving configuration changes without restarting upstream. A commonly repeated extra rationale is that 5 s is roughly the time before the system could flag an ANR so work is not cut mid-flight; treat that rationale as folklore and verify before quoting it. The round number is not a platform constant.

When the timeout elapses the upstream flow is cancelled, but the StateFlow keeps its last value; on the next subscription the upstream restarts and re-emits. With replayExpirationMillis default (infinite) the last value is replayed immediately, so the UI shows stale state instantly then updates. The initialValue (Loading) only shows before the first emission ever.

combine semantics (A1 has operators): emits only after every source has emitted once; then emits on every upstream emission using the latest of each. If one upstream never emits, combine never emits and the UI stays in Loading.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class BooksViewModel @Inject constructor(
    repo: BooksRepository,
    userData: UserDataRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val query = MutableStateFlow("")

    val uiState: StateFlow<BooksUiState> = combine(
        repo.observeBooks(),             // Flow<List<Book>> from Room, hot-ish
        userData.observeBookmarks(),     // Flow<Set<BookId>>
        query,
    ) { books, bookmarks, q ->
        BooksUiState.Content(
            items = books.filter { it.title.contains(q, ignoreCase = true) }
                .map { it.toRow(bookmarked = it.id in bookmarks) },
            query = q,
        )
    }.stateIn(
        scope = viewModelScope,
        started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
        initialValue = BooksUiState.Loading,
    )

    fun onQuery(q: String) { query.value = q }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Eagerly for everything: keeps DB observers and sockets alive while the app is in the background.
  • WhileSubscribed() (timeout 0): every rotation tears down and restarts upstream, causing flicker and repeat network (Q031).
  • Reading uiState.value in init or in a function when nobody subscribes: with WhileSubscribed the value is still initialValue.
  • Doing one-shot work (a POST) inside the combine lambda.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the UI is on the back stack, not destroyed? → The collector (lifecycle-aware) stops at STOPPED, 5 s later upstream stops; on return it restarts. Use Lazily or a longer timeout if restart is expensive.
  2. Why stateIn rather than asLiveData or shareIn? → StateFlow has a current value, equality-based conflation, and works in KMP; shareIn has no value semantics.
  3. How do you test this? → Collect in backgroundScope with an UnconfinedTestDispatcher, otherwise WhileSubscribed never starts and value stays at initial (Q047).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: copy the sample. Senior: explains the three policies' upstream lifetimes, what the 5 s is for, combine's first-emission gate, and the testing consequence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped WhileSubscribed(5000) for Eagerly "to fix a loading flash" and later traced a battery-drain report to a Room observer plus a polling flow running for every opened screen in the background.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 8.14 of a food-delivery app (3.4M DAU, 62% Android 11-14 mid-range devices). Within 24 hours: the restaurant list screen sends 2 to 3 identical GET /restaurants calls per open (API cost alert: +41% on that endpoint, from 18M to 25.4M calls/day), rotating the phone shows a blank spinner for about 600 ms, and a dev sees in Logcat RestaurantsViewModel: collecting nearby repeating on each rotation. The change in 8.14 was "cleanup stateIn usage" in RestaurantsViewModel:

val uiState = combine(repo.nearby(), prefs.sort()) { r, s -> Content(r.sortedWith(s)) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), Loading)

repo.nearby() is a cold flow that calls the API on collection, then emits cached results.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate and prevent. What do you ship today and what do you change structurally?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a cache with Retrofit/OkHttp" or "use Eagerly". The first hides the architectural cause; the second keeps the API polling in the background and wastes the quota differently. They do not connect the unsubscribe timing of rotation to stopTimeoutMillis = 0.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the diff change from WhileSubscribed(5_000) to default? (blame says yes). Is the 2-3x a function of rotations or of navigation return? Does nearby() trigger a network call per collection or is there a repository-level cache? Which collection API does the UI use (collectAsState vs collectAsStateWithLifecycle)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cherry-pick a one-line fix: SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000). Staged rollout to 5% (Play Console staged rollout) and compare calls/open. Server-side, enable a short-TTL CDN/response cache on that endpoint if available.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stopTimeoutMillis = 0: rotation destroys the collector for a few ms, upstream is cancelled, resubscription restarts repo.nearby() which re-calls the API. (b) The UI collects with plain collectAsState and also restarts when the NavHost entry recomposes. (c) A duplicate init { } fetch alongside the flow. (d) OkHttp retry interceptor. Red herring: the prefs.sort() DataStore flow; it is local.
  4. How I'd verify each: Charles/Proxyman or OkHttp HttpLoggingInterceptor counting requests per rotation; a test that collects, cancels for 50 ms, re-collects and asserts one repository call; Logcat marker on upstream onStart; compare 8.13 versus 8.14 diff.
  5. Root cause: With the default timeout 0, when the Activity is recreated the subscriber count hits 0, the sharing coroutine is cancelled immediately, and re-subscribing restarts the whole cold upstream including its network call. Because the initial value is Loading, the replay cache is reset for the new started cycle, hence the 600 ms spinner (replay expiration default is infinite, but the screen was also paying for the network wait before the first fresh emission being treated as loading in the repository's own onStart { emit(Loading) }).
  6. Fix: Short term: restore WhileSubscribed(5_000). Long term: separate "observe cache" from "refresh": the repository exposes a local-DB Flow and a refresh() suspend; the ViewModel triggers refresh once per screen entry, not per collection.
val uiState = combine(repo.observeNearby(), prefs.sort()) { r, s -> Content(r.sortedWith(s)) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Loading)

init { refresh() }   // once per ViewModel, not per collection (idempotent, see Q047 for init rules)
fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch { repo.refreshNearby() }
  1. Prevention: A unit test "resubscribe within 5 s does not call the repo twice"; dashboard on API calls per screen open; code review rule that stateIn always names its SharingStarted and timeout.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Eagerly or Lazily as a quick fix; they remove the stop-in-background behaviour. Moving refresh to init means rotation is free but a long-lived ViewModel in the back stack will not refresh on return; for that I add a stale-while-revalidate TTL check in the repository.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the product wants refresh each time the screen returns to foreground? → Trigger refresh() from a lifecycle ON_START effect with a minimum interval, not from flow collection.
  • How does the 5 s interact with a 6 s process in the background? → Upstream stops after 5 s; return re-collects; acceptable if the first value is from DB.
  • Could replayExpirationMillis help? → It limits how long the last value is replayed after upstream stops; default is Long.MAX_VALUE, so no change needed here (verify exact default in the kdoc).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "tidy-up" PR deleted what looked like a magic number and tripled traffic to a search endpoint; finance noticed before engineering did. The fix was a one-line revert, the lasting change was a ViewModel test asserting call counts across a simulated rotation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests adding HTTP caching or Eagerly.
  • Hire: Links rotation to timeout 0 and restores 5_000.
  • Strong hire: Also separates refresh from observation, adds the resubscribe test, and measures with API-per-open.

questions.promptHtml: Why must UiState be immutable, and how do List, var properties and non-Kotlin-module types in UiState affect Compose skipping?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It joins architecture to rendering performance. A senior knows a UiState that "looks" immutable can still be unstable for the compiler.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Immutability gives the single-writer guarantee: if state objects cannot change, a new value means a new reference, StateFlow's equality check works, and no composable sees a half-mutated state. For Compose, a parameter type must be stable for the compiler to skip recomposition when inputs are equal. List<T> is an interface the compiler cannot prove immutable, so it is treated as unstable and a composable taking it recomposes more than needed. Fixes: kotlinx.collections.immutable types, a stability configuration file, or relying on strong skipping, which is the default from Kotlin 2.0.20's Compose compiler (verify for your version)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two separate reasons for immutability:

  1. Architecture. StateFlow conflates and compares with equals. If you mutate an ArrayList inside the state and re-emit the same reference, equals is trivially true, nothing is emitted (Q048). In-place mutation also races with the collector reading on another thread.
  2. Compose skipping (A3 has details). The compiler infers a class as stable if all public properties are val of stable types (primitives, String, function types, stable classes). var properties or List/Set/Map (read-only interfaces which could be backed by mutable implementations) make it unstable. Unstable params: a composable is skipped only if the instance is the same (===) rather than equal. With strong skipping (default in newer compiler: verify the exact version for your setup), all composables become skippable, unstable params compared by instance equality, stable by equals, and lambdas are auto-remembered. That reduces but does not erase the problem: each emission that creates a new List instance triggers recomposition even if contents are equal.

Types from other modules are the second stability hole: a class from a non-Compose module is considered unstable unless the module applies the compiler or you list it in the stability configuration file. Tools: Compose compiler reports/metrics (-P plugin:...:reportsDestination) show stable/unstable/skippable.

Practical rules: val everywhere; ImmutableList/PersistentList from kotlinx.collections.immutable (or @Immutable/@Stable annotations as promises, which the compiler trusts, so a lie causes missed updates); map to row models whose equals is cheap and stable; use item key.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Immutable
data class FeedUiState(
    val items: ImmutableList<FeedRow> = persistentListOf(),
    val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
)

// Broken: mutable inside "immutable" data class
data class BadUiState(val items: MutableList<FeedRow>)          // equals sees same ref after mutation
class Bad2(var count: Int)                                       // var => unstable, and UI may read torn state

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Immutable on a class that holds a MutableList: a promise the compiler cannot check; updates are skipped.
  • Converting List to ImmutableList in the composable (items.toImmutableList()) every recomposition: allocates and defeats skipping.
  • Domain models with Date or Android types in UiState.
  • Assuming data class means stable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does strong skipping make ImmutableList unnecessary? → Mostly for parameters passed unchanged, but new list instances with equal contents still recompose; ImmutableList's equality semantics help only with stable comparison, so measure with the compiler reports.
  2. How do you find unstable classes? → Compose compiler metrics and reports, plus Layout Inspector recomposition counts.
  3. Should the ViewModel produce ImmutableList? → Convert at the pipeline's map, once, off the UI thread.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "data class + val". Senior separates the architecture reason from the compiler reason, names the List instability, annotation risk, strong-skipping caveat and verifies with compiler reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search results screen re-composed all 60 visible rows on every typed character because List<SearchRow> was unstable under the old compiler; switching to ImmutableList cut recompositions from ~60 to ~2 per keystroke in Layout Inspector.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between collectAsState and collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and which should a ViewModel's StateFlow use in an Android app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A simple check that you know a collector in Compose keeps running while the app is backgrounded unless you tell it not to, and how that connects to WhileSubscribed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "collectAsState collects as long as the composable is in the composition, even if the Activity is stopped, so upstream work continues in the background. collectAsStateWithLifecycle from lifecycle-runtime-compose starts collecting at STARTED by default and cancels at STOPPED, so combined with WhileSubscribed the upstream stops. On Android I use the lifecycle-aware one for ViewModel flows."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The pipeline lifecycle contract in Google's guidance: state production must not consume resources when the UI is not visible. Two links make that true:

  • Producer side: stateIn(..., WhileSubscribed(5_000)) tears upstream down when there are no subscribers.
  • Consumer side: the collector must actually go away when the UI is stopped. collectAsState does not: composition lives while the Activity is stopped (composition is disposed with the view tree, not at ON_STOP), so the subscriber count never drops and WhileSubscribed never stops upstream.

collectAsStateWithLifecycle uses repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) internally (parameter minActiveState, default STARTED), re-subscribing on return. It needs an initial value only when the receiver is a plain Flow; for StateFlow it uses value. Available in lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.6+ (verify for your BOM).

Differences that matter: with collectAsState in a KMP/Compose Multiplatform common source set you cannot use the lifecycle variant on all targets (the lifecycle artifacts are multiplatform in newer versions; verify). Outside Android UIs, use collectAsState.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun FeedRoute(vm: FeedViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    FeedScreen(state, vm::onRefresh)
}

Broken: val state by vm.uiState.collectAsState() while the ViewModel pipeline holds a location/socket flow; backgrounded app keeps the radio busy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using LaunchedEffect { flow.collect { } } to push into local state: no lifecycle awareness.
  • Thinking collectAsStateWithLifecycle loses state when stopped: it keeps the last State value; only collection pauses.
  • Collecting the same flow in three composables of one screen, tripling subscribers (they share the StateFlow but each is a collector).
  • Hoisting the collection too low and recomposing the whole screen on every emission.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does that behave with Lifecycle.State.RESUMED? → Use minActiveState = RESUMED to avoid collecting while a dialog or multi-window partially covers the app; costs freshness.
  2. What does the user see on return? → Last state immediately, then updates when collection resumes.
  3. Where to collect in a nav graph? → At the route-level composable, pass plain state down (A3 covers state hoisting).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "lifecycle aware, so better". Senior ties it to WhileSubscribed: both halves are needed for resource release, and explains why collectAsState leaves the subscriber count high.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fitness app with collectAsState kept a heart-rate stream upstream alive in the background for hours; the battery-historian profile showed it, switching to the lifecycle variant stopped it after 5 s.

questions.promptHtml: Where should transformations live: repository, domain/use case, ViewModel, or composable? Give me a rule, not "it depends".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Misplaced mapping creates either a bloated ViewModel or leaks of UI concerns downward. A rule shows judgment under ambiguity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "My rule: transform at the lowest layer that has all the information and none of the presentation concerns. Data shape conversion (DTO to domain) in the repository. Business rules reused by more than one screen in domain. Screen-specific shaping into what a screen needs, like grouping, filtering by the current query, view models of rows, in the ViewModel's pipeline off the main thread. Anything that needs Context, locale, resources, window size or theme, last, in the UI, because that is UI logic and lifecycle dependent."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Test each transformation with three questions:

  1. Does it need UI-lifecycle data (Resources, locale-dependent formatting, Context, density)? Then UI layer. If you format "$12.50" in the ViewModel with NumberFormat.getInstance(), a runtime locale change leaves stale text, and you tempt an Application Context into the ViewModel.
  2. Is it reused across screens or a business rule ("order is refundable if delivered < 30 days ago")? Domain/use case or a pure function in the data layer. Google keeps the domain layer optional: add it for reuse and complexity, not for ceremony.
  3. Is it screen-specific shaping (filter by the typed query, merge two streams, section headers)? ViewModel, in the combine/map pipeline, run with flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) when it costs.
 DB/API -> [repo: DTO->domain] -> [domain: rules] -> [VM: shape for screen] -> [UI: format with Resources]
 pure data, no UI concept      reuse, testable      testable w/o Android      locale/theme/density

Cost consideration: a mapping per emission scales with list size. For 5k rows and a 20 ms map, doing it in the composable's body adds 20 ms to each recomposition frame (frame budget at 60 Hz is about 16.7 ms), a guaranteed jank; in the pipeline it runs once per upstream change.

Boundary types: UiState should hold what rendering needs, with stable primitives and domain value types (Money, Instant), with the final string produced in the UI or via a UI-text abstraction (a sealed UiText resolved with a Context in the composable).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UiText {
    data class Res(@StringRes val id: Int, val args: List<Any> = emptyList()) : UiText
    data class Plain(val value: String) : UiText
}
@Composable fun UiText.asString(): String = when (this) {
    is UiText.Res -> stringResource(id, *args.toTypedArray())
    is UiText.Plain -> value
}
// ViewModel never touches Context:
_state.update { it.copy(message = UiText.Res(R.string.err_network)) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• ViewModel takes Application to call getString(): locale change shows stale text; tests need Robolectric.
  • Mapping in the composable body without remember.
  • Domain layer that merely forwards repo calls ("use case per method").
  • Putting screen-specific sorting into the repository, so another screen needs a different order and forks it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A runtime locale or font-scale change: what breaks first? → Anything pre-formatted in the ViewModel; hence raw values or UiText.
  2. Does moving mapping off Main fix everything? → It fixes the frame cost but you still pay allocation; map incrementally for huge lists.
  3. How do you stop the god-ViewModel as shaping grows? → Extract pure mapper functions or a domain use case, keeping the ViewModel as orchestration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "mapper in the ViewModel". Senior gives a decision rule with three tests, explains the locale/lifecycle argument, accounts for frame budget, and keeps the domain layer justified by reuse.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app formatted dates in the ViewModel with the device locale at creation time; users who switched language at runtime saw mixed languages until process restart.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketplace search screen on mid-range devices (4 GB RAM, Snapdragon 6-series; 38% of users). Product list up to 5,000 items from Room; filters: query text, 6 facet chips, sort, price range slider, "in stock only". Telemetry: p95 frame time 38 ms while typing, jank 14% of frames, slider drag drops to ~20 fps, ANR rate 0.31% on this screen (threshold 0.47% per Play vitals bad-behavior bar for user-perceived ANR, verify), a trace shows 60 ms on the main thread inside combine lambda. Code:

val uiState = combine(repo.products(), query, facets, sort, priceRange, inStock) { p, q, f, s, r, st ->
    SearchUiState(
        items = p.filter { it.matches(q, f, r, st) }.sortedWith(s.comparator())
            .map { it.toRow() },
        query = q, facets = f, sort = s, range = r, inStock = st,
    )
}.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState())

Every typed character and every slider tick re-runs the whole thing; the list composable receives a new List<Row> each time.
questions.promptHtml: The screen is janky on mid-range devices. How do you restructure the state production?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add debounce" or "use remember". Debounce helps text but not the slider; they do not move work off Main nor stop re-filtering the DB result when only the slider moved; they do not address list identity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is repo.products() all 5,000 rows or already filtered in SQL? Is the price slider continuous or committed on release? Does the UI need results live while dragging? Is the list paged visually or is it all in memory? What is the target frame time (16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apply debounce(150) to the text only and commit the slider on onValueChangeFinished (hotfix, no architecture change). Add flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) to the combine so the 60 ms leaves Main.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Filtering and sorting in Kotlin on all rows per input change, on Main, because stateIn's upstream runs in viewModelScope (Main.immediate) unless flowOn. (b) Mapping to Row allocations: 5k objects per keystroke, GC pressure. (c) New list instance forces all visible rows to recompose (Q032). (d) Slider emits at frame rate into the same combine.
  4. How I'd verify each: System Trace / Perfetto for main-thread slices in combine; Android Studio CPU profiler; allocation profiler for Row count per keystroke; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; JankStats frame data.
  5. Root cause: Work proportional to full dataset (n = 5000) on the main thread at input rate; no distinction between inputs that need SQL re-query, in-memory re-filter or only a presentation change.
  6. Fix: Push filtering and sorting into the DB with a flatMapLatest over a parameter object, debounce text, run the pure mapping on Dispatchers.Default, and hand the UI an ImmutableList of stable rows with keys. Keep the control values (query, slider position) in their own cheap state so the text field never waits on the pipeline.
private val criteria: Flow<Criteria> = combine(query.debounce(150), facets, sort, committedRange, inStock, ::Criteria)
    .distinctUntilChanged()

val results: StateFlow<ImmutableList<Row>> = criteria
    .flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }                 // SQL WHERE/ORDER BY, cancels stale queries
    .map { list -> list.map(Product::toRow).toImmutableList() }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), persistentListOf())
// Controls state is separate: query text and slider position update the UI instantly
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric for typing and scrolling on a low-end device in CI; perf budget (e.g. p95 frame < 20 ms); a baseline profile; lint review rule against heavy work in combine lambdas without flowOn.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Paging unless 5k grows toward 50k; I would not debounce so long that search feels laggy (150 ms is a typical starting point; tune with data). Splitting controls from results state accepts a short window where the query shows new text and results are old; it is better than a laggy text field, and an isSearching hint covers it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Search is server-side instead of Room: same shape, but flatMapLatest cancels in-flight HTTP; add a tiny local cache.
  • 50k items: use Paging 3 with PagingSource per criteria; cachedIn(viewModelScope).
  • Why distinctUntilChanged after combine? → Equal criteria (e.g. slider jitter after rounding) must not re-query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team spent a sprint on remember tweaks before a trace showed 70% of the frame was a Kotlin filter on the main thread; a 20-line pipeline change dropped jank from 14% to 2%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use debounce", cannot read a trace.
  • Hire: Moves work off Main, debounces, commits slider on release.
  • Strong hire: Distinguishes input classes, pushes filtering to SQL, uses flatMapLatest, stable list types, separates control state from result state, defines a perf budget in CI.

questions.promptHtml: What are the failure modes of combine when producing UiState from several streams (initial emission gate, error in one source, cancellation, slow source), and how do you design around each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: combine is recommended by Google for most cases, and it hides three production traps. Seniors should know them by heart.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "combine emits nothing until every source has emitted once, so one silent source leaves the UI in Loading forever. An exception in any source cancels the whole combined flow and terminates state production, so I catch per source and turn failures into data. A slow source delays the first state, so I give optional sources a default with onStart { emit(default) } or model them as Async states inside the UiState."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Semantics: combine(a, b) { x, y -> } collects both concurrently; emits after each has produced at least one value; afterwards emits on every upstream emission with the latest values. Completion happens when all complete. Failure: an exception in any upstream cancels siblings and the collector fails.

Design rules:

  1. First-emission gate. If b is "user bookmarks" that may legitimately take 2 s or never emit for guests, the whole screen waits. Use b.onStart { emit(emptySet()) } or stateIn it with a default, or make the part nullable-with-meaning (Loading) in the UiState so the screen renders partially (Q045).
  2. Errors as data. Per source: repo.items().map<_, Result>{ Success(it) }.catch { emit(Failure(it)) }. Otherwise one failing source kills the StateFlow upstream; with stateIn the exception propagates into viewModelScope's coroutine and (no CoroutineExceptionHandler) crashes the app.
  3. Cancellation is not an error. catch receives cancellation only for downstream-induced exceptions in some cases; do not swallow CancellationException in runCatching inside the lambda.
  4. Fan-in rate. Each source emission re-runs the lambda: five chatty sources means five recomputations; conflate() or debounce on noisy inputs, distinctUntilChanged on each source.
  5. More than 5 sources. The typed overloads go up to 5 flows (verify); beyond that use combine(listOf(...)) which loses types, or nest/group sources into sub-states.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private fun <T> Flow<T>.asLoadable(): Flow<Loadable<T>> =
    map<T, Loadable<T>> { Loadable.Ready(it) }
        .onStart { emit(Loadable.Loading) }                    // do not gate the screen on this source
        .catch { emit(Loadable.Failed(it.toUiError())) }       // error becomes data, upstream survives

val uiState = combine(
    repo.profile().asLoadable(),
    repo.recommendations().asLoadable(),
    repo.notifications().asLoadable(),
) { p, r, n -> HomeUiState(p, r, n) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), HomeUiState())

Broken: three raw flows combined; if recommendations() throws a SocketTimeoutException, the exception escapes and the screen crashes or freezes at its last value depending on handling.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming combine emits partial results.
  • A single catch after combine: it ends the flow; the screen freezes with no recovery path.
  • Using zip (pairs emissions 1:1) by mistake.
  • Heavy work inside the lambda per emission.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. combine vs merge + scan? → merge + scan (reducer) gives you ordering and per-event semantics; useful for MVI; combine is for latest-value state.
  2. How to retry just one source? → retryWhen on that source or a trigger flow it flatMapLatests from, not on the combined flow.
  3. How does the screen show partial data? → Each source is Loadable<T> in the state; UI renders sections independently.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use combine". Senior lists the gate, error propagation and noisy-input problems with specific operators to mitigate each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home screen sat at a skeleton for guests because the "saved items" flow only emitted for logged-in users; onStart { emit(emptyList()) } fixed a 9% bounce on first launch.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement optimistic updates in a UDF architecture (like, follow, add to cart), and where does the truth live while the request is in flight?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It exposes whether you understand single source of truth under concurrency: rollback, ordering, retries and reconciliation with the server.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I apply the change immediately to the local source of truth, the database or repository cache, and mark it pending, then send the request. On success I reconcile with the server's response; on failure I roll back to the last confirmed value and surface an error. The UI only renders the repository's state, so there is no separate 'optimistic copy' in the ViewModel. The hard parts are ordering of rapid toggles, rollback that does not clobber newer user intent, and idempotency of retries."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two designs:

  1. ViewModel-local overlay. The ViewModel keeps pendingLikes: Map<Id, Boolean> and merges it over repository data in combine. Simple, but the optimistic value dies with the ViewModel and other screens showing the same item disagree.
  2. Repository/DB as single source of truth. The repository writes liked = true, syncState = PENDING locally, emits it to all observers, then syncs. Every screen agrees; process death does not lose the intent if the pending op is persisted (a queue, WorkManager is A5's detail).

Correctness issues:

  • Rapid toggles: like, unlike, like in 300 ms. Serialize per-entity operations (a per-key Mutex or a Channel) or coalesce to the final desired state; otherwise responses arrive out of order and the last response, not the last intent, wins.
  • Rollback to what? Roll back to the last confirmed value, not blindly !current, since a newer toggle may already be pending.
  • Idempotency: send desired state (PUT /likes/{id} {liked:true}), not a delta (POST /toggle), so retry or duplicates are safe.
  • Reconciliation: the server response (count 1,204 vs your guess 1,203) replaces the local guess; avoid UI jump by animating.
  • Failure UX: error message through state (Q045), item returns to prior value.
tap -> local: liked=true,pending   -> UI shows liked immediately
         \-> network PUT
              ok  -> local: confirmed=true, pending=false, count=server
              err -> local: liked=confirmed(old), pending=false, error to UI

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class LikesRepository(private val dao: PostDao, private val api: PostApi) {
    private val locks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Mutex>()

    suspend fun setLiked(id: String, liked: Boolean) {
        val mutex = locks.getOrPut(id) { Mutex() }
        // 1) optimistic write is immediate and unlocked so the UI reacts now
        dao.setLikedPending(id, liked)
        mutex.withLock {                       // 2) per-item serialization of network calls
            val desired = dao.desiredLiked(id) // latest intent, not the captured argument
            try {
                val r = api.putLike(id, desired)           // idempotent desired-state call
                dao.confirm(id, r.liked, r.likeCount)
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                dao.rollbackToConfirmed(id)
                throw e
            }
        }
    }
}

Broken: ViewModel does state = state.copy(liked = !state.liked), calls api.toggle(id), and on error does copy(liked = !liked) again; double taps flip it twice and responses race.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Delta APIs (toggle) under retry.
  • Rollback using a captured stale snapshot.
  • Optimistic state stored only in rememberSaveable/composable, invisible to other screens.
  • Forgetting to handle ViewModel/scope cancellation: use an application-scoped repository scope for writes that must finish.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When not to be optimistic? → Payments, irreversible actions, server-validated outcomes with frequent rejection.
  2. How to show "pending" to the user? → A syncState in the row model: subtle indicator or none for cheap actions.
  3. What if the app is killed after the optimistic write? → Persist the pending op and retry on next launch (durable queue); without it, the local value diverges from the server.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: update state, call API, revert on error. Senior: places truth in the repository/DB, serializes per entity, uses idempotent desired-state calls, and reconciles with the server value.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Likes flickered in a feed because out-of-order responses to rapid taps applied stale counts; per-item serialization plus server-count reconcile fixed support tickets.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app, 900k DAU. Since 5.20, "follow" button users report: "I followed, it shows following, then after a minute it says Follow again" (about 2.3% of follow taps, up from 0.1%). Server logs show PUT /follow 200 OK for those users. The failure correlates with: poor connectivity, and users who tap follow then quickly open that profile's page. Client code:

fun onFollow(id: String) {
    val before = state.value.authors.first { it.id == id }
    _state.update { s -> s.copy(authors = s.authors.map { if (it.id == id) it.copy(following = !it.following) else it }) }
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try { api.toggleFollow(id) }
        catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { s -> s.copy(authors = s.authors.map { if (it.id == id) before else it }) } }
    }
}

OkHttp has retryOnConnectionFailure(true) (default) and one app-level retry interceptor (up to 2 retries) on IOException.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and fix it without a full rewrite.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The catch rolls back, so make the call succeed" or "increase timeouts". They miss that the server toggled twice because of the retry on a non-idempotent endpoint, and that the local flag was flipped by ! instead of set explicitly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is /follow really a toggle (server flips state) or does it take a desired value? Does the retry interceptor apply to POST/PUT? Does the profile page read the same state or call its own GET /author? Are there duplicate requests per tap in the server log (same user, same id, within seconds)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side kill-switch or client remote flag to disable the retry interceptor for non-GET calls; ship a client hotfix to disable app-level retries on this endpoint. Rollout staged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Non-idempotent toggle plus a retry after a response lost on a flaky network: the server flipped twice, ending unfollowed, then the next fetch shows "Follow". (b) Profile page fetch races: it loads the author with following=false from a read replica lagging behind the write. (c) The client's local !following plus rollback to a captured before overwrites a newer update. (d) Duplicate taps. Red herring: the 200s in logs, which prove the request reached the server, not that its effect was applied once.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query server logs for two PUT /follow with the same client request id spacing near the retry interval (OkHttp event listener shows retry counts); reproduce with network link conditioner dropping the response (not the request); unit test with a fake API that succeeds but throws after applying.
  5. Root cause: A non-idempotent toggle API behind a transparent retry path. The ambiguous failure case (server applied, client never saw the 200) was handled as "retry", and the retry flipped it back. Client-side, the state model also stores a delta, not intent.
  6. Fix: Short term: no retries on mutating non-idempotent calls (OkHttp's default retry on connection failure applies only to failures where the request was not delivered, but the app interceptor did not discriminate). Long term: change the contract to desired state with an idempotency key, and keep the intent as data.
// API: PUT /authors/{id}/follow  body { following: true }   (idempotent), header Idempotency-Key
fun onFollow(id: String, desired: Boolean) {
    _state.update { it.withFollowing(id, desired, pending = true) }
    viewModelScope.launch {
        runCatching { api.setFollowing(id, FollowBody(desired), idempotencyKey = UUID.randomUUID().toString()) }
            .onSuccess { r -> _state.update { it.withFollowing(id, r.following, pending = false) } }
            .onFailure { e ->
                if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                _state.update { it.revertPending(id) }
            }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Contract test that mutating endpoints are idempotent (or carry an idempotency key); a lint/review rule on retry interceptors being limited to idempotent methods; an end-to-end test with a flaky proxy; metric "follow reversal within 5 min".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove optimistic UI; the fix is idempotency and serialization (Q037). I would not keep a client-only workaround (de-duplicating taps) since a retry still doubles server effects. Backend change needs a coordinated release with a client fallback for old versions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old app versions still call the toggle: keep both endpoints; server dedupes by (user, target, 2 s window) temporarily.
  • The server cannot change this quarter: client queues one in-flight call per item and, after any ambiguous failure, GETs actual state before retrying.
  • What does revertPending roll back to? → The last confirmed value stored alongside the pending one, not !current.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "retry everything" interceptor added during a latency push quietly turned a toggle into a coin flip for users on trains; the finding came from a user-research clip, not metrics, until we added reversal-rate tracking.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames network or adds a longer timeout.
  • Hire: Finds the retry on a toggle and the ! delta; proposes desired-state calls.
  • Strong hire: Adds idempotency keys and per-item serialization, handles the ambiguous-success case, ships a mitigation first, and instruments reversals.

questions.promptHtml: How do you model list state with pagination (initial load, append loading, append error, end reached, refresh)? Paging 3 or hand-rolled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real feeds are all pagination. They probe whether you can model the extra states, avoid duplicate page requests, and know when a library is justified.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A list screen has two orthogonal pieces: the items, and the load status for each direction: refresh (initial/pull), append (next page). I model that explicitly rather than one isLoading. For anything non-trivial I use Paging 3, which gives LoadStates per direction, cachedIn(viewModelScope), retry and remote mediator support. I hand-roll only for simple cursor lists, and then I guard against duplicate requests with one in-flight job and an endReached flag."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State to represent:

items: [..................]
refresh: NotLoading | Loading | Error     (first load / pull-to-refresh)
append:  NotLoading(endReached=false|true) | Loading | Error   (footer)

Paging 3 exposes CombinedLoadStates (refresh, prepend, append, plus source/mediator) and LazyPagingItems in Compose via collectAsLazyPagingItems(). The ViewModel exposes Flow<PagingData<Row>> built with Pager(config, pagingSourceFactory).flow.map { it.map(::toRow) }.cachedIn(viewModelScope). cachedIn is required so rotation does not refetch and so multiple collectors share. PagingData is not a UiState you can copy; to merge UI-only state (selected, filters) you transform the PagingData with map/filter, or keep selection in a separate state keyed by id.

Hand-rolled: keep nextCursor, isAppending, endReached; a loadNext() that ignores calls when isAppending || endReached; trigger from scroll position through snapshotFlow of last visible index (prefetch distance, e.g. 5 items from the end).

Deduplication: pages may overlap after inserts on the server; dedupe by stable id with distinctBy when appending, or use keyset pagination. Always provide key = { it.id } in LazyColumn.

Rule for choice: Paging 3 when you need DB-backed paging with RemoteMediator, placeholders, or many states; hand-roll when you have a cursor list that fits in memory and tests must be trivial. Paging internals and Room integration live in A5.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface PageStatus { data object Idle : PageStatus; data object Loading : PageStatus; data class Error(val msg: String) : PageStatus }

data class FeedUiState(
    val items: ImmutableList<FeedRow> = persistentListOf(),
    val refresh: PageStatus = PageStatus.Loading,
    val append: PageStatus = PageStatus.Idle,
    val endReached: Boolean = false,
)

fun loadNext() {
    val s = _state.value
    if (s.append is PageStatus.Loading || s.endReached || job?.isActive == true) return
    _state.update { it.copy(append = PageStatus.Loading) }
    job = viewModelScope.launch { /* fetch(cursor), then update items, append=Idle, endReached = page.isLast */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One isLoading for refresh and append: the full-screen spinner appears at the bottom of a long list.
  • Triggering loadNext() from composition (LaunchedEffect(lastIndex) without guards): double fetch.
  • Replacing the list on refresh with an empty Loading.
  • Forgetting cachedIn: rotation refetches page 1 and scroll position is lost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Append failed: what does the user see? → Footer with retry, items stay; no full-screen error.
  2. Pull-to-refresh with prepend items? → Preserve scroll anchor by id, not index.
  3. How do you hold a filter plus paging? → Filter in a flatMapLatest creating a new Pager per filter value; cachedIn after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Paging 3". Senior: states per direction, guards against duplicates, cachedIn, anchor stability and a rule for when not to use the library.

sections.label: Production connection
