sections.html: A comments screen double-appended page 3 under fast fling because loadNext had no in-flight guard; the duplicate rows broke LazyColumn with "Key was already used" crashes at about 0.4% sessions.

questions.contextHtml:
A feed (page size 20, next cursor from the API) crashes with IllegalArgumentException: Key "post_8812" was already used. If you are using LazyColumn/LazyRow please make sure you provide a unique key for each item. in 0.6% of sessions, mostly right after pull-to-refresh on a fast network. Also reported: "after refresh I sometimes see the end of the list twice". Code:

class FeedViewModel(private val repo: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _items = MutableStateFlow<List<Post>>(emptyList())
    val items: StateFlow<List<Post>> = _items
    private var cursor: String? = null

    fun loadMore() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val page = repo.page(cursor)
            _items.value = _items.value + page.posts
            cursor = page.next
        }
    }
    fun refresh() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            cursor = null
            _items.value = repo.page(null).posts
            cursor = ...
        }
    }
}
// UI: LazyColumn { items(items, key = { it.id }) { PostRow(it) } }; scroll to bottom calls loadMore()
questions.promptHtml: Find every defect, explain the crash and the duplicated tail, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use distinctBy in the UI" or "remove the key". The first treats a symptom, the second hides it and breaks item state and animation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can loadMore be triggered more than once at the end of the list? Does a refresh invalidate in-flight loadMore? Can the server reorder or insert between pages (cursor stability)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add distinctBy { it.id } at the merge point as a stop-gap, ship quickly; it stops the crash without changing behaviour.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Race: loadMore (cursor=A) is in flight; user pulls to refresh; refresh sets state to page1, then the old loadMore completes and appends page2 of the old list (or page1 re-appended), producing duplicate ids and a stale cursor. (b) Fast scroll triggers loadMore twice with the same cursor, appending the same page twice. (c) Server inserts an item between requests, so offset-style pages overlap. (d) The cursor = ... in refresh is incomplete (cursor stays null so next loadMore reloads page 1 and appends).
  4. How I'd verify each: Fake repo with CompletableDeferred to hold a loadMore, call refresh(), release: assert final list has unique ids; unit test double loadMore(); check scroll-trigger code path; log cursor values per call.
  5. Root cause: Unsynchronized, non-cancellable page loads mutating shared items and cursor, with no in-flight guard and no generation or job identity, so completion order determines state.
  6. Fix: One job at a time, refresh cancels append, set cursor and items atomically in one state.
data class FeedState(val items: List<Post> = emptyList(), val cursor: String? = null,
                     val endReached: Boolean = false, val appending: Boolean = false)

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(FeedState())
private var loadJob: Job? = null

fun loadMore() {
    val s = _state.value
    if (s.appending || s.endReached) return
    _state.update { it.copy(appending = true) }
    val requested = s.cursor
    loadJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        val page = repo.page(requested)
        _state.update { cur ->
            if (cur.cursor != requested) cur                       // stale completion: ignore
            else cur.copy(items = (cur.items + page.posts).distinctBy { it.id },
                          cursor = page.next, endReached = page.next == null, appending = false)
        }
    }
}
fun refresh() {
    loadJob?.cancel()
    loadJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        val page = repo.page(null)
        _state.value = FeedState(page.posts, page.next, page.next == null)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Test for overlapping refresh/append and double append; crash alert on "Key ... already used"; lint on missing key; instrumentation to count loadMore per scroll.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop the key (it preserves item state and animations). distinctBy is O(n) per page; fine for hundreds of items, for thousands I keep a HashSet of ids or move to Paging 3 (Q039).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cancelling refresh job mid-request: should the cancelled loadMore leave appending = true? → No: it must reset in finally/on cancellation, or refresh replaces whole state anyway.
  • Users scroll up during append: use stable keys and no index-based scroll restoration.
  • Rate-limit by server: the guard also protects the API quota.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 0.6% crash kept recurring because three separate fixes "deduplicated" in the UI; the real cause was two in-flight page loads with different cursors.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Removes the key or dedupes in UI only.
  • Hire: Finds the double load, adds an in-flight guard and cancels on refresh.
  • Strong hire: Also ignores stale completions via cursor check, atomic state, deterministic race tests, and states when to move to Paging 3.

questions.promptHtml: How do you model form state (fields, validation, submit status), and why does a TextField bound to a ViewModel StateFlow sometimes jump the cursor or drop characters?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Forms mix fast synchronous state with slow validation and submit. The cursor-jump question is a known Compose trap that signals real hands-on experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I keep each field's raw input as state that updates synchronously on every keystroke, and derive validation and canSubmit from it. The submit status is a separate sealed state. The cursor jump comes from routing keystrokes through an async hop: the TextField asks the ViewModel for the new value, the ViewModel publishes it through a StateFlow collected on a later frame, and meanwhile the TextField recomposes with the stale value, so the IME and the composable's text disagree and the cursor or characters get lost. Fix: update the state synchronously, either with Compose State/TextFieldState, or keep a local mutableStateOf in the UI and push the value to the ViewModel."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Form model:

data class SignUpFormState(
    val email: String = "",
    val password: String = "",
    val emailError: EmailError? = null,   // set after blur or submit attempt, not on every keystroke
    val submit: SubmitState = SubmitState.Idle,
) {
    val canSubmit get() = email.isNotBlank() && password.length >= 8 && submit !is SubmitState.Submitting
}
sealed interface SubmitState { data object Idle: SubmitState; data object Submitting: SubmitState; data class Failed(val msg: String): SubmitState; data object Done: SubmitState }

Validation timing is product design: validate on blur or on submit attempt, then live-revalidate once an error is shown; validating on every keystroke yells at users mid-typing. Cross-field rules (confirm password) derive from the state. Server errors (email taken) are field-level errors stored per field.

The cursor issue: Compose's TextField(value: String, onValueChange) is a controlled component and expects the new value to be applied in the same frame. With MutableStateFlow and collectAsStateWithLifecycle, the emission is delivered via a coroutine dispatch (and StateFlow conflation), so the value the TextField renders can lag behind IME input, particularly with fast typing, Dispatchers hops or debounce. Google's own text-field state post and docs recommend mutableStateOf (or a state backed by Compose snapshot state) for text fields (the state-production page itself says to use mutableStateOf especially with Compose text APIs). Newer BasicTextField with TextFieldState (Compose Foundation 1.7+, verify) removes the controlled-component round trip entirely.

Process death: form input is user-typed data that is lost on process death unless saved (Q043); rememberSaveable for local text or SavedStateHandle.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SignUpViewModel(savedState: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    var form by mutableStateOf(SignUpFormState(email = savedState["email"] ?: ""))
        private set

    fun onEmail(v: String) {                    // synchronous, same-frame
        form = form.copy(email = v, emailError = if (form.emailError != null) validateEmail(v) else null)
    }
    fun onSubmit() { /* validate all, set Submitting, launch call, set Done/Failed */ }
}

Broken: onEmail(v) { viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { _state.update { it.copy(email = v) } } }: the text lands later than the IME expects.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Updating text state from a background dispatcher.
  • Debouncing the text value instead of the validation (debounce the derived check, never the displayed text).
  • Clearing the whole form on a server error.
  • Showing "invalid email" on the first keystroke.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does validation logic live? → Pure functions in domain/ViewModel, unit-testable; the UI only renders error enums mapped to strings.
  2. Async validation (username availability)? → Debounced flatMapLatest over the field, result stored as Checking | Available | Taken.
  3. Multi-step forms across screens? → Shared state holder scoped to the flow (nav graph ViewModel), persisted via SavedStateHandle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: MutableStateFlow<String> per field. Senior: names the cursor jump mechanism, picks synchronous text state, models validation timing and submit status separately, and covers process death.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login screen with a 200 ms debounce on the field value dropped characters for fast typists on low-end phones; moving debounce to validation only fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: You join a fintech team. PM brief: "Design the state for the new KYC screen: name, DOB, address (autocomplete from an API), ID photo upload, T&C checkbox. Users abandon at 31% right now. It should feel instant, validate properly, never lose what they typed, and the Continue button should only be enabled when valid. Compliance says server validation is authoritative." No other detail. Support is on 20% of devices under 3 GB RAM; the flow takes a user about 4 minutes and many switch apps to fetch their ID.
questions.promptHtml: Before writing code, how do you clarify and then design the UI state model?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A data class with fields and a ViewModel with StateFlow." No questions, no process death, no server validation, no photo upload state, and canSubmit as the only gate.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must typed data survive app kill (low-memory devices switching to a camera or gallery app suggests yes)? Are validation rules client-computable or server-only? Can the user continue with an upload in progress? Is the photo upload resumable and how large (5 MB or 20 MB)? Should Continue be disabled when invalid or enabled with inline errors (disabled buttons hide why)? Legal: can partial PII be persisted to disk, and is it encrypted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design task). The "mitigation" is a thin vertical slice: name and DOB fields plus save/restore, to show the state model before the full form.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: For the 31% abandonment: (a) lost data after app switch (process death while taking a photo); (b) errors shown late or only after Continue; (c) opaque disabled button; (d) slow address autocomplete.
  4. How I'd verify each: Funnel analytics per step; session replay on the abandon step; reproduce with "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill while the camera is open; measure autocomplete latency.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The design principle is that the form state is user-owned data that must survive, and its parts have different lifecycles.
  6. Fix (design):
data class KycFormState(
    val name: FieldState = FieldState(),
    val dob: FieldState = FieldState(),
    val address: AddressState = AddressState.Empty,       // sealed: Empty | Typing(q, suggestions: Loadable) | Selected(Address)
    val idPhoto: PhotoState = PhotoState.None,            // sealed: None | Local(uri) | Uploading(progress) | Uploaded(id) | Failed(retryable)
    val acceptedTerms: Boolean = false,
    val submit: SubmitState = SubmitState.Idle,
    val serverErrors: Map<FormField, String> = emptyMap(),
) {
    val isComplete get() = name.valid && dob.valid && address is AddressState.Selected &&
        idPhoto is PhotoState.Uploaded && acceptedTerms
}
data class FieldState(val value: String = "", val error: FieldError? = null, val touched: Boolean = false) {
    val valid get() = value.isNotBlank() && error == null
}

Persist only primitive inputs in SavedStateHandle (name, DOB, selected address id, photo URI or upload id) and not the whole object; autocomplete suggestions are re-derivable. Because it is PII, persist drafts only if compliance allows, else keep to in-memory and process-death restore via SavedStateHandle (Bundle, which is in-memory and never written to disk by the app, verify the platform's own persistence of saved state). Validation: client rules for format; server errors mapped back to fields; Continue always tappable, tapping reveals errors and scrolls to the first (accessible and instructive). Upload runs independent of the ViewModel scope (WorkManager/foreground upload service is A5) and reports progress via the repository. 7. Prevention: Process-death instrumented test per step; analytics on field-level error rate; screenshot tests for each PhotoState. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hold the whole form as one monolithic copy() target if it grows; split into step states. I would not store raw PII in disk-backed drafts without explicit compliance sign-off. I would not disable Continue silently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compliance says no drafts at all: then rely on in-memory restore only and explain the abandonment risk to the PM with numbers from the kill test.
  • The address API is slow (p95 2 s): debounce 300 ms, show previous suggestions with a subtle loading state, allow manual entry.
  • Two-pane tablet layout: the same state, a different composable layout (UI logic).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a KYC drop-off fell from 31% to 24% after one change: restoring typed data after a camera round trip killed the process on 3 GB devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Writes a flat data class with no questions.
  • Hire: Asks about process death and server validation, models upload and submit status.
  • Strong hire: Designs state per lifecycle (user input, derived validity, async parts), handles PII constraints, tests with process kill, and prioritizes by the funnel data.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to UiState on configuration change versus process death, and how do you decide what to save and restore?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most apps are only tested with rotation. Senior candidates design for the system killing the process while the app is in the background, and understand the size and identity constraints.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A ViewModel survives configuration change but not process death. After the system kills the backgrounded process, the user returns to a recreated Activity and nav back stack with a brand new ViewModel. I save the minimum needed to rebuild the screen, such as ids, query text, selected tab and unsaved form input, in SavedStateHandle, and re-derive everything else from the data layer. I do not save big lists or objects: saved state goes through a Bundle with a size limit around 1 MB shared across the process's transactions, and it is the wrong place for data that the repository can reload."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lifetimes:

Event Activity ViewModel remember rememberSaveable / SavedStateHandle
Rotation Recreated Kept Lost Kept
Process death (background kill) Recreated New instance Lost Restored from the saved-state Bundle
User swipes away / finish() Destroyed Cleared Lost Dropped

Mechanism: the system calls onSaveInstanceState before the Activity may be killed; SavedStateHandle is backed by the same saved state registry, so its values are written into the Bundle, which is handed to the system (ActivityManager) and later returned on re-creation. Nav destination arguments and NavBackStackEntry state are restored the same way.

What to save (rule): inputs that cannot be re-derived and identity that lets you re-derive the rest:

  • Save: entity ids (productId), search query, sort option, selected tab, scroll anchor id, unsaved form text, a draft id.
  • Do not save: lists loaded from the repository, UiState as a whole, bitmaps, big domain objects, anything that includes Throwable, lambdas or Android views.
  • Restore: on re-creation the pipeline uses the saved ids to reload from the DB/network. Google's guide says the same: the saved handle provides the minimum information to restore UI state from the data layer.

Practical API: SavedStateHandle.getStateFlow(key, initial) makes a saved value an observable flow; savedStateHandle.saveable { } property delegates and rememberSaveable with a Saver exist for composite objects (check the exact artifact version for the delegate: verify). Values must be Bundle-compatible: primitives, Parcelable, Serializable; with kotlinx.serialization you can write a custom Saver.

Size and cost: transactions across Binder share a buffer of about 1 MB per process; exceeding it throws TransactionTooLargeException (an Android runtime exception that also appears as a crash at background time, not in the screen you wrote). Budget: a few KB per screen, and the saved state of all Activities and fragments counts together.

Test it: enable "Don't keep activities" (this recreates the Activity but does NOT kill the process, so it does not test ViewModel loss) and, properly, adb shell am kill <package> with the app backgrounded, then reopen from recents.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class ProductViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val saved: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repo: ProductRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val productId: String = checkNotNull(saved["productId"])           // nav arg, restored by Navigation
    val query = saved.getStateFlow("query", "")                                // survives process death

    val uiState: StateFlow<ProductUiState> = combine(repo.observe(productId), query) { p, q ->
        ProductUiState.Content(p.toUi(), q)
    }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProductUiState.Loading)

    fun onQuery(q: String) { saved["query"] = q }
}

Broken: saved["items"] = state.items with 3,000 elements.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only rotation.
  • Believing "Don't keep activities" simulates process death for ViewModels.
  • Saving the entire UiState as Parcelable "to be safe".
  • Passing a full object as a navigation argument so there is nothing to re-derive from after restore (Q044 style crash).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not persist everything to Room instead? → Drafts the user would expect to survive days belong in disk; saved state is for transient UI continuity and is cleared when the task is removed.
  2. How does this interact with WhileSubscribed? → Restored ids kick off upstream when the UI collects; there is no separate restore step.
  3. What about rememberSaveable inside a LazyColumn item? → Needs stable keys, otherwise state is attached to the wrong item.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use SavedStateHandle". Senior: gives the lifetime table, the save-ids-not-data rule, the Bundle limit, and the correct way to test process death.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An e-commerce app lost the checkout address step after users switched to a banking app on low-RAM devices, and crash dashboards showed NullPointerException where a singleton-held draft was expected; saving a draft id and reloading fixed both.

questions.contextHtml: Vitals shows a new crash cluster after release 12.3: java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1,048,912 bytes from ActivityThread$StopInfo.run, affecting 0.8% of sessions (about 14k users/day of 1.7M DAU), nearly all on backgrounding (user presses Home). No stack frames from your code. A second cluster, in the same release: IllegalStateException: Required value was null in OrderDetailViewModel.<init> after returning from the background, only on devices with 3 GB RAM or less. 12.3 changed order details: the nav argument is now a @Parcelize data class OrderArg(val order: Order) (order with up to 60 line items and product thumbnails as ByteArray), and the ViewModel does private val order = savedStateHandle.get<OrderArg>("order")!!.order.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both crashes and fix them without breaking deep links or the existing navigation graph.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch TransactionTooLargeException" (you cannot, it happens in the framework), "compress the bitmaps", or treating the null crash as an unrelated bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the average size of OrderArg? Is the same Order also placed in other Bundles (fragments, saved state of other screens)? Does the null crash correlate with process death (check "was app in background > N min")? Are order objects available from the repository by id?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote kill for the heaviest part: stop sending thumbnails in the Parcelable (hotfix ship), and pass only orderId. If the release is staged, halt the rollout at current percentage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The saved-state Bundle of the Activity (nav args, saved state of every back stack entry) exceeds about 1 MB at onStop; the order details with ByteArray thumbnails dominate. (b) The null crash: after process death, Navigation restores the entry's arguments but a custom field the code wrote elsewhere (not saved) is missing or the argument parcel was dropped by an earlier truncated save. (c) Multiple Order screens in the back stack each hold a large arg. Red herring: device RAM, which only affects how often the process dies, not the Bundle size limit.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the Bundle size at onSaveInstanceState in a debug build (Parcel.obtain().apply { writeBundle(b) }.dataSize()), or use Android Studio's profiler/StrictMode; reproduce with several order screens stacked; adb shell am kill with the app backgrounded; inspect the nav graph arguments.
  5. Root cause: Domain/UI data was passed as a navigation argument, so it lives in the saved-state Bundle that goes through Binder when the Activity stops; large objects exceed the transaction limit (about 1 MB shared across all pending transactions in the process; verify exact limit for the API level). The null crash is a separate consequence of treating the argument as an always-present in-memory object and of partial restoration differences when the save is dropped or the screen was entered by a path that did not include the full object.
  6. Fix: Short term: pass only the id; the ViewModel loads from the repository.
// Route: orderDetail/{orderId}  (or a type-safe @Serializable data class OrderDetail(val orderId: String))
@HiltViewModel
class OrderDetailViewModel @Inject constructor(
    saved: SavedStateHandle,
    repo: OrderRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val orderId: String = checkNotNull(saved["orderId"])
    val uiState = repo.observeOrder(orderId)
        .map<Order, OrderDetailUiState> { OrderDetailUiState.Content(it.toUi()) }
        .catch { emit(OrderDetailUiState.NotFound) }                // missing id is a state, not a crash
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), OrderDetailUiState.Loading)
}

Long term: a project-wide rule "navigation args are ids and small primitives". Thumbnails stay in the image cache keyed by URL. If the repository is network-only, cache the order locally so restore does not require the network. 7. Prevention: A lint or Detekt rule flagging Parcelable classes with collections or ByteArray in nav args; a debug-build Bundle size logger that warns above, say, 200 KB; a CI test that kills the process on each screen; crash alert on TransactionTooLargeException. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise any limits (there is no app-controlled limit) or split Bundles. Id-only args cost a lookup (milliseconds from Room), and "not found" must be a first-class state. I would not keep a singleton cache as the source for the object after restore: it is empty after process death.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Deep link arrives with an order id the user does not own: the ViewModel returns NotFound/Forbidden via state, not an exception.
  • The product wants an instant render with the data from the list screen: the repository's in-memory cache provides it, and the id-based load is the fallback.
  • Can we compress the Parcelable? → It helps by a constant factor but the failure shape (growth with data) remains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a crash looked random until we noticed it only occurred after the user had opened 4+ detail screens; each carrying a modest object, the sum crossed the limit at backgrounding.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Tries to catch the exception or shrink images.
  • Hire: Recognizes Bundle size limit and switches to id-only args.
  • Strong hire: Explains the aggregated saved state at onStop, fixes the null crash through state-as-data, adds Bundle size monitoring and process-kill tests.

questions.promptHtml: How should a screen render partial data and errors (stale data with a failed refresh, one failed section on an otherwise healthy screen, empty vs error)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps rarely have "all or nothing" data. The design shows whether you model failures per part and can say what the user should see in each case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Errors are scoped to the thing that failed. If I have data, a refresh failure is a banner or snackbar, not a blank screen. If a secondary section fails, that section shows an inline retry while the rest renders. Only when there is nothing to show does the full-screen error appear. I model it by giving each independently loadable part its own Loadable state, and distinguishing 'empty' from 'failed' from 'not loaded yet'."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision table:

Situation What the user should see State shape
First load, no cache, failed Full-screen error + retry Error(message) top-level
Cache exists, refresh failed Cached content + non-blocking message Content(items, refreshError)
One of three sections failed Other sections normal, that section inline retry section: Loadable<T> per part
Loaded, zero results Empty state (different copy/CTA than error) Content(items = []) with isEmpty derived
Offline, cache stale by 3 days Content + "last updated 3 days ago" Include lastUpdated: Instant

Per-part model:

sealed interface Loadable<out T> {
    data object Loading : Loadable<Nothing>
    data class Ready<T>(val value: T, val stale: Boolean = false) : Loadable<T>
    data class Failed(val error: UiError, val lastValue: Any? = null) : Loadable<Nothing>
}

Error type: map exceptions to a small UI-facing taxonomy (Offline, Timeout, Server, Unauthorized, Unknown) in the data/ViewModel boundary; the UI chooses copy and action (retry, sign-in). Do not put Throwable or e.message in state; messages are not localized, not stable, may leak internals, and Throwable is not equals-friendly.

Transient messages (snackbar for refresh failure) follow Google's "events become state" guidance: store userMessage in state, show it, then notify the ViewModel to clear it (details in the one-off events chunk). Persistent banners are plain state.

Retry semantics: retry only re-runs the failed part (flatMapLatest on a per-section retry trigger), never the whole screen; automatic retry uses backoff and stops (data layer's job; A5).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class HomeUiState(
    val header: Loadable<Header> = Loadable.Loading,
    val feed: Loadable<ImmutableList<Card>> = Loadable.Loading,
    val recommendations: Loadable<ImmutableList<Card>> = Loadable.Loading,
    val refreshError: UiError? = null,
)

@Composable
fun Section(l: Loadable<ImmutableList<Card>>, onRetry: () -> Unit) = when (l) {
    Loadable.Loading -> SectionSkeleton()
    is Loadable.Ready -> CardRow(l.value, showStaleHint = l.stale)
    is Loadable.Failed -> InlineError(l.error, onRetry)        // contained, not full screen
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating empty list and error the same ("No items" for a failed load).
  • Replacing content with a spinner on every refresh.
  • One error: String? for the whole screen when three independent calls exist.
  • Auto-retry loops that hammer a failing backend (cost and battery).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you represent "loaded from cache while revalidating"? → Ready(value, stale = true) plus a refreshing flag; the repository emits cache first, then network (A5 details).
  2. Unauthorized mid-session? → That is app-wide state (session), not a per-screen error; route to sign-in via the session layer (see the app-wide state chunk).
  3. How do you test the matrix? → Preview/screenshot test per state and a ViewModel test per transition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: one Error screen. Senior: scopes failures to parts, keeps stale data visible, distinguishes empty vs error vs unloaded, and defines a UI error taxonomy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home screen showed a full-page error when only the recommendations API had an outage, hiding a perfectly healthy feed; per-section failure raised the session length during that outage.

questions.contextHtml: A 6-year-old app, 2.1M DAU, 90 screens. The ViewModels use flag-style states (isLoading, error, data) and a mix of LiveData and StateFlow. A quarterly audit lists 41 bugs in the last two quarters tied to "impossible states" (spinner plus error, empty flash before data). Leadership wants these gone, but you have 7 engineers, 40% of capacity for tech debt, and the release train is every 2 weeks. Crash-free is 99.6%; a regression on checkout costs about 0.8% of daily revenue per day of impact.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate UiState modelling across 90 screens safely without a rewrite freeze?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite all ViewModels to sealed states this quarter" or "just do it screen by screen" with no ordering, no safety net and no stopping criteria.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens produce the 41 bugs (are they concentrated in 8 screens)? Are tests present at ViewModel level? Is the UI Compose, Views or mixed? Can we ship behind a flag per screen? What is the revenue-critical set (checkout, login)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the worst offenders only, apply a surgical fix (e.g. clear error when loading starts) without remodelling, to stop the bleeding while the migration plan lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The bugs are Pareto-concentrated in 10 to 15 screens with complex async. (b) Many "bugs" come from three shared patterns (refresh handling, error clearing, LiveData/StateFlow mixed collection), fixable with a shared helper. (c) The true cause is missing transition tests; remodelling alone will not stop regressions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tag the 41 bugs by screen and pattern; count flags per ViewModel via a script (grep isLoading + error); check test coverage on those ViewModels; review how many screens are touched weekly (churn).
  5. Root cause: An unconstrained state shape and no transition tests, so each author invents semantics for flag combinations.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Phase 0 (1 sprint): Write the target: a documented state template (exclusive modes sealed, orthogonal facts fields: Q026), a Loadable helper, a UI error taxonomy, and Compose previews per state. Agree in an ADR.
    • Phase 1: Characterization tests on the top 10 buggy ViewModels (record current emissions for fake repos), then migrate each behind the same public behaviour; ship per screen on the train with a remote flag for the riskiest (the old path remains until the metric is clean).
    • Phase 2: Opportunistic migration: "touch it, migrate it" rule for any screen with a feature change; no big-bang.
    • Phase 3: Add a Detekt/custom lint rule flagging new ViewModels with two or more mutually exclusive booleans and LiveData/StateFlow mixing; stop-loss: when the monthly bug count from state modelling falls under 3, stop proactive migration. Bridging code: keep the old UiState and add a mapper OldState.toNew() so UI can move first, ViewModel later, or the reverse, per screen.
// Adapter during migration: UI renders the new model; old ViewModel still exposes flags
fun OrdersLegacyState.toUi(): OrdersUiState = when {
    error != null && orders.isEmpty() -> OrdersUiState.Error(error.toUiError())
    isLoading && orders.isEmpty() -> OrdersUiState.Loading
    else -> OrdersUiState.Content(orders, isRefreshing = isLoading, refreshError = error?.toUiError())
}
  1. Prevention: The lint rule, PR template item "state shape reviewed", a screenshot test per state, and a quarterly bug-by-pattern review.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not migrate low-churn, low-bug screens: the cost has no payoff. I would not mix migration with UI redesigns (two variables). Sealed states slightly increase boilerplate and need Compose smart-cast handling; I accept that for exhaustiveness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Product demands a feature in a not-yet-migrated screen: do the migration in the same PR if under a day; otherwise add the feature with the adapter and file a tracked task.
  • How do you prove it worked? → Bugs per quarter tagged "state" drop 41 to under 10, and crash-free and revenue guardrails unchanged.
  • Half the team prefers MVI: align on state shape (the outcome), not on the library; MVI-with-reducer can fit the same template.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the team ran a "state hygiene" campaign, migrated 12 of 90 screens, and cut state bugs by 80% because the 12 screens were where the bugs lived; the other 78 were never touched.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Proposes a freeze and rewrite or has no safety net.
  • Hire: Prioritizes by bug concentration, adds tests first, migrates incrementally.
  • Strong hire: Adds adapter bridging, a lint guardrail, flags for risky screens, an explicit stop-loss metric, and the ADR/alignment.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test a ViewModel whose UiState comes from combine(...).stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000))? Why is vm.uiState.value often just the initial value in tests?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates have flaky or vacuous ViewModel tests. The WhileSubscribed testing trap is a precise, common pain point.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With WhileSubscribed, the upstream only runs while something collects, so a test that reads .value without a subscriber sees initialValue forever. I start a collector in backgroundScope using an UnconfinedTestDispatcher, set Dispatchers.Main to a test dispatcher, drive fakes with MutableSharedFlow or MutableStateFlow, and assert on the sequence of states with Turbine or by reading .value after runCurrent(). I inject dispatchers and use fakes, not mocks, so the test is about behaviour."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Ingredients:

  • Main dispatcher: viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate; replace with Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) via a JUnit rule (MainDispatcherRule) and reset after (kotlinx-coroutines-test, A1 for the test APIs).
  • Subscribe: stateIn(WhileSubscribed) starts only with a subscriber. In runTest, backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect {} }; backgroundScope is cancelled at the end of the test so the 5 s timeout does not leave a running coroutine (which would otherwise make runTest wait/fail on active coroutines).
  • Virtual time: the 5_000 ms timeout uses virtual time; advanceTimeBy(5_001) verifies the upstream stops.
  • Fakes over mocks: a FakeOrdersRepository with MutableStateFlow/MutableSharedFlow and controllable errors; tests read like scenarios: emit data, assert Content; emit error, assert state.
  • Turbine: uiState.test { assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem()); ... } checks emission sequence; remember StateFlow conflation means you may not see every intermediate value, only the settled ones when running on an unconfined dispatcher.
  • Dispatcher injection: inject CoroutineDispatcher (or a provider) into repositories/use cases rather than hardcoding Dispatchers.IO; use the test scheduler.

Rule on init: do not launch work in init that the test cannot control; Google warns against async work in init or the constructor (leaking this, ordering with Compose state). Use stateIn laziness or an idempotent initialize().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainDispatcherRule(private val d: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(d)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}

class BooksViewModelTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule()
    private val repo = FakeBooksRepository()               // exposes MutableSharedFlow
    private val vm = BooksViewModel(repo, FakeUserData())

    @Test fun showsContentWhenRepoEmits() = runTest {
        backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect() }  // starts upstream
        assertEquals(BooksUiState.Loading, vm.uiState.value)
        repo.emit(listOf(book("1")))
        assertEquals(1, (vm.uiState.value as BooksUiState.Content).items.size)
    }
}

Broken: val s = vm.uiState.value with no collector, asserting Content: it fails or, worse, passes against a handwritten initial value.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dispatchers.setMain forgotten: IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize.
  • Using delay with real time.
  • first() on a StateFlow, which returns the initial value instantly.
  • Mocking the repository with strict verifies, coupling to implementation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test that upstream stops after backgrounding? → Cancel the collector job, advanceTimeBy(5_001), assert the fake repo's subscription count is 0.
  2. How do you test a SavedStateHandle ViewModel? → Construct SavedStateHandle(mapOf("id" to "1")) directly.
  3. How do you test the rendering of every state? → Screenshot or Compose UI tests (the testing chunk covers strategy).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: Mockito and .value. Senior: explains the WhileSubscribed subscriber requirement, backgroundScope, virtual time for the timeout, and fakes with controllable flows.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's "green" ViewModel tests all asserted Loading because no collector was attached; a regression sailed through until QA caught a blank screen.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for "tasks screen does not update after check-off": 310k users affected, 2.9% of sessions saw it for 3 days (release 4.8, no crashes, support tickets: "I tick a task and nothing happens until I leave and come back"). Timeline: 4.7 used immutable lists; 4.8 changed the ViewModel for "performance" (avoid copying lists). A reviewer approved because tests passed (they assert on the list contents).

data class TasksUiState(val tasks: MutableList<Task> = mutableListOf(), val isLoading: Boolean = false)

class TasksViewModel(private val repo: TaskRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(TasksUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<TasksUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun onChecked(id: String) {
        val s = _state.value
        s.tasks.first { it.id == id }.done = true          // Task has var done
        _state.value = s                                    // "emit" the same object
        viewModelScope.launch { repo.setDone(id, true) }
    }
}
// Compose: TaskList(state.tasks) where TaskList(tasks: List<Task>)
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: why did it break, why did tests and review miss it, what do we change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use copy()" and stop. It skips the detection gap (why tests pass), the Compose angle, and process prevention.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why was "performance" the motivation, and was it measured? Which screens use the same pattern? Did any test collect the flow and check emissions or just contents? Why did it only affect 2.9% of sessions (not 100%)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix 4.8.1: replace in-place mutation with copying; staged rollout; in-app message or server config to force a refresh is not needed once the screen updates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StateFlow ignores a value equal to the current one; _state.value = s is the same reference, so equals is true and nothing is emitted. (b) Even if emitted, Compose receives the same List instance and cannot know it changed (mutable list is not snapshot-observed), so it does not recompose. (c) Why only 2.9%: the screen refreshes from the repository on return and when other changes occur (new list instance), masking the bug for most flows, so only the "check and stay" path is broken.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test collecting state and asserting a second emission after onChecked; log System.identityHashCode; Layout Inspector recomposition count unchanged after a tap.
  5. Root cause: Mutable state inside the UiState plus re-assignment of the same reference. The unidirectional loop was broken: the ViewModel changed state without producing a new value, so the framework had nothing to propagate.
  6. Fix: Immutable model and copy-on-write, optimistic with rollback (Q037).
data class Task(val id: String, val title: String, val done: Boolean)
data class TasksUiState(val tasks: ImmutableList<Task> = persistentListOf(), val isLoading: Boolean = false)

fun onChecked(id: String) {
    _state.update { s -> s.copy(tasks = s.tasks.map { if (it.id == id) it.copy(done = true) else it }.toImmutableList()) }
    viewModelScope.launch { repo.setDone(id, true) }
}

For long lists, persistentListOf().set(index, ...) gives structural sharing, avoiding the O(n) copy that motivated the "optimization". 7. Prevention: Detekt rule/Konsist test: no var or MutableList in classes named *UiState (architecture tests are in the testing chunk); test helper that asserts a new emission occurs after each action; review checklist "state objects are immutable"; Compose compiler report in CI to catch unstable params. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blame the reviewer: tests passed because they asserted contents, not emissions. Copying 200 tasks is microseconds; I would measure before accepting any "performance" justification; for 20k elements I would use persistent collections or Paging.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could mutableStateListOf have worked? → In Compose it is snapshot-observable and would recompose, but it ties the ViewModel to Compose runtime, and cross-thread mutation needs snapshots; fine if deliberate, not as an accident.
  • What if the repo returns a Flow of the DB rows? → Then the checkbox writes to the DB and the UI updates from the flow; no manual state mutation.
  • How do you catch this class earlier? → Property: for every action, state before != state after, in ViewModel tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team lost three days of reports to the same pattern in a settings screen; the fix was a 3-line copy, the real work was making immutability a compile-time or lint-time guarantee.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use copy" only.
  • Hire: Explains StateFlow equality and Compose's inability to see in-place mutation.
  • Strong hire: Explains the detection gap, proposes persistent collections for performance, adds lint/architecture tests and a measured-performance rule in review.
